summary:
Charter publishes a piece by Kristen Berman of Irrational Labs arguing that workers fear AI job loss broadly but exempt themselves. Press coverage (WSJ, Washington Post, The Atlantic) has made AI job anxiety a defining workplace story of the year, with tech workers reportedly staying in jobs they dislike for fear of no alternatives.

Irrational Labs surveyed 150 employees, half in the technology industry. Only 15% thought AI was likely to eliminate their own job within a year, and about a third expected elimination within three years. By contrast, 67% expected AI to take peers' jobs within a year (4.5x the rate predicted for themselves), and three-quarters expected peer impact within three years versus 32% for themselves (a 2.3x gap). The author notes these findings mirror a Pew survey of 5,273 people, in which roughly a third expect AI to reduce their own long-term job opportunities and a similar share expect little difference.

Two cognitive biases are offered as explanations: optimism bias (citing psychologist Tali Sharot on underestimating personal risk of divorce, cancer, car accidents) and the better-than-average effect (a classic 1981 study, recently replicated, where 93% of American participants rated their driving above the median).

The piece then argues for a "Goldilocks" amount of fear using the Yerkes-Dodson law: too little concern breeds complacency, too much causes freezing or tool-chasing without strategy. Leaders should not send alarmist all-caps mandates; instead, regular hands-on AI exposure makes the threat concrete and converts vague fear into specific skill questions.

Finally, respondents estimated they capture only 45% of AI's potential on average. Tech and non-tech respondents answered nearly identically, suggesting proximity to the technology does not increase felt competence. The clearest split was gender: men estimated 50% versus 43% for women. The closing advice is to use AI tools more and feel uncomfortable working exactly as before.
